title: Linear Algebra
subject: Linear Algebra
summary: Strang's linear algebra from elimination to the SVD, with a deliberate detour into complex vectors, Hermitian and unitary matrices, and function spaces. This is the language of quantum mechanics (states are vectors, observables are Hermitian matrices), of normal modes in classical mechanics, and of the molecular-orbital and Hückel calculations the chemist already knows.

units.title: Vectors, Systems and Elimination
units.summary: Linear systems seen three ways (rows, columns, matrices), solved by elimination, packaged as A = LU.

lessons.title: Vectors, Linear Combinations and Matrices as Column Combinations
objectives: Form linear combinations of vectors and sketch the span of one, two and three vectors in R^2 and R^3.
Compute dot products, lengths and angles, and use the Cauchy-Schwarz and triangle inequalities to bound them.
Write Ax as a combination of the columns of A, and explain why this view (not the row-by-row dot-product view) is the one that generalises.
Interpret Ax = b as the question 'is b in the span of the columns of A?'.
keyEquations: A x = x_1 a_1 + x_2 a_2 + \dots + x_n a_n

State that matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative and give a physical example of non-commuting operations (e.g. rotations).
Find A^{-1} by Gauss-Jordan elimination and decide when an inverse exists.
Prove (AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1} and explain the order reversal.

Compute the nullspace N(A) by elimination, identifying pivot and free variables and writing the special solutions.

Explain why rank determines solvability and the number of free parameters.

Find bases for all four subspaces of a given matrix, using R and the row operations E with EA = R.
Apply the rank-nullity relation r + (n - r) = n to explain a concrete counting argument.
Show that a rank-1 matrix is a column times a row, and decompose a matrix as a sum of rank-1 pieces.

units.title: Orthogonality, Projections and Least Squares
units.summary: Orthogonal subspaces, projection onto a subspace, least-squares fitting (the chemist's linear regression), Gram-Schmidt and QR.

lessons.title: Orthogonality of the Four Subspaces
objectives: Show that the row space is perpendicular to the nullspace, and the column space to the left nullspace.
Define the orthogonal complement and state that the two pairs split R^n and R^m into perpendicular parts.
Decompose any x as a row-space part plus a nullspace part, and explain what A does to each.
Explain why A^T A is invertible exactly when A has independent columns.

lessons.title: Projections and Least-Squares Fitting

Show P^2 = P and P^T = P, and explain what P does to vectors in C(A) and in N(A^T).
Derive the normal equations A^TA x_hat = A^Tb by minimising ||Ax - b||^2 and by geometry.
Fit a line and a parabola to data by least squares, and interpret the residual as orthogonal to the column space.
Connect to chemistry: calibration curves and Beer-Lambert regression are least-squares projections.

Write A = QR and interpret R as the record of the Gram-Schmidt coefficients.

units.title: Determinants
units.summary: Determinants as signed volume, with the properties and formulas that physics calculations (secular equations, cross products, Jacobians) lean on.

lessons.title: Determinant Properties and Formulas
objectives: State the three defining properties of det and derive the others (row exchange flips sign, det of product, det of transpose, singular iff 0).
Compute determinants by elimination (product of pivots) and by cofactor expansion along a row.
Use the big formula (sum over permutations) to see why a 3x3 determinant has six terms.
Explain det(AB) = det(A)det(B) and its consequence det(A^{-1}) = 1/det(A).

lessons.title: Cramer's Rule, Inverse Formula and Volume
objectives: Write A^{-1} = C^T/det A and solve small systems by Cramer's rule, noting why it is not a practical algorithm.
Show |det A| is the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the rows (or columns) of A.
Relate the Jacobian determinant of a change of variables to the volume scaling factor, tying back to multivariable calculus.

units.title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
units.summary: The central topic for physics: diagonalisation, powers, linear ODE systems and the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices (normal modes; Hückel MO theory).

lessons.title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
objectives: Define Ax = lambda x and interpret it geometrically as a direction that A only stretches.
Compute eigenvalues from det(A - lambda I) = 0 and eigenvectors from the nullspace of A - lambda I for 2x2 and 3x3 matrices.
Prove trace = sum of eigenvalues and det = product of eigenvalues.
Explain what complex or repeated eigenvalues mean (rotations; defective matrices).
Connect to chemistry: the Hückel secular determinant is an eigenvalue problem for the pi-orbital energies.

units.title: Complex Vectors, Hermitian and Unitary Matrices
units.summary: Linear algebra over C: Hermitian and unitary matrices are the observables and time evolution of quantum mechanics.

Explain why QM observables are Hermitian (real measured values) and time evolution is unitary (probability conserved).
Connect to chemistry: spin-1/2 states and the NMR two-level Hamiltonian are 2x2 Hermitian eigenproblems.
